articles.title_zh: China fires kindergarten principal, warns officials over ‘mops in pots’ scandal
articles.content_orig:
Whistle-blower expresses relief upon seeing the announcement, saying, ‘The children there can eat clean food now’
Local Chinese authorities have issued warnings and demerits to 11 officials and dismissed the entire kitchen staff at a kindergarten following a teacher’s revelation about unsanitary practices, including washing dirty mops in cooking pots.
On June 30, several children at the Affiliated Kindergarten of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology in Jiangsu province exhibited symptoms such as nausea and vomiting during and after lunch.
Parents had been inquiring about the kindergarten’s hygiene throughout the summer break, but they received no official response until September.

articles.title_orig: China's factory activity returns to growth in September amid AI boom
articles.title_zh: China's factory activity returns to growth in September amid AI boom
articles.content_orig:
China's factory activity returned to growth in September as a deepening economic malaise prompts policymakers to ramp up stimulus steps and bolster growth.
The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index rose to 50.1 from 49.8 in August , National Bureau of Statistics data showed Wednesday, in line with analysts' forecast for a modest expansion of 50.1 in a Reuters poll.
Manufacturers in the country have benefited from the AI hardware boom, while weak consumer demand at home has been a major worry, with higher energy costs owed to the Middle East war weighing on margins.
Exports have been one of the few drivers of China's economy this year, but that engine is showing signs of strain as trading partners voice growing concerns over the country's excess manufacturing capacity and heavy reliance on foreign demand, while domestic consumption lags.
China's top economic and financial policymakers on Tuesday unveiled targeted fiscal and monetary measures to lower financing costs and boost central bank lending, as Beijing calls for stronger counter-cyclical support to keep the economy on track to meet its full-year growth target.
"The new round of supportive measures is not sufficient to bolster growth," a team of economists at Nomura wrote in a note, adding that the steps were too small to address the real barriers to growth.
"The measures are more significant as a policy signal than as a near-term growth impulse," Goldman Sachs economists echoed. Targeted credit easing mainly supports the supply side, and whether it translates into investment and broader growth will depend on how the policies are implemented, they said.
The mortgage subsidy announced Tuesday is more direct support for housing demand and may lift home sales in the short term, Goldman added. With the program set to run for one year, it could also pull forward some first-home purchases, Goldman analysts said.

articles.title_orig: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.title_zh: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.
Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.
“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.
The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.
A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats , who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.
When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

“Glee” alum Harry Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson earned a 24/30 for their Jive to the hit “You Make My Dreams (Come True),” while “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” alum Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik scored a 21/30 for their Quickstep to the duo’s “Maneater.”
Elsewhere, “Save the Last Dance” actress Julia Stiles — who got emotional over low scores and a rib injury this week — and partner Ezra Sosa’s Salsa to the Hall & Oates classic “I Can’t Go for That (No Can Do)” garnered them a 19/30.
The group Toto also saw two of their songs represented, with Olympian gold medalist Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov earning a 24/30 for their Foxtrot to “Hold the Line,” and “Step Up” actress Jenna Dewan and partner Val Chmerkovskiy scoring a 21/30 for their Samba to the band’s hit “Africa.”

Talks between the two leaders in Washington produced a string of joint announcements, but some say it was more about managing tensions
But some American China watchers said the results fell short of a major breakthrough and were more about managing tensions than resolving the fundamental differences between the two countries.
Mike Kuiken, vice-chair of the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told the South China Morning Post that the summit was largely about “how do we hold the status quo in place”.
“I just don’t expect breakthroughs,” Kuiken said. “I think every breakthrough – which I would argue is probably most likely to be incremental – is going to be through hard-fought diplomatic discussions and negotiation.”

articles.title_zh: The Red Sox and Yankees are underway in the Bronx. Follow live updates.
articles.content_orig:
Baseball’s most storied rivalry writes another chapter on Tuesday when the Red Sox and Yankees meet in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series.
Boston finds itself in a rare position. After falling short to the Yankees a season ago in this same round, the Red Sox are back in the Bronx and looking to flip the script in the best-of-three series. These two teams have been on a collision course throughout September. The Yankees won the season series 7-6.
Payton Tolle gets the ball for the Red Sox, opposing Walpole’s Cam Schlittler and the Yankees.
Globe reporters Peter Abraham, Tim Healey, and Alex Speier are coming to you live from Yankee Stadium with insight and analysis. Follow along throughout the game.
RED SOX (87-75): Anthony DH, Rutschman C, Contreras 1B, Abreu RF, Rafaela CF, Sogard 2B, Duran LF, Story SS, Durbin 3B
Pitching: LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA)
YANKEES (93-68): Goldschmidt 1B, Rice DH, Ramos RF, Bellinger LF, Lombard Jr. SS, Rosario 3B, Volpe 3B, Jones CF, Wells C
Pitching: RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA)
Time: 8 p.m. | TV, radio: NBC, Peacock, WEEI-FM 93.7
Red Sox vs. Schlittler: Wilyer Abreu 2-9, Willson Contreras 1-12, Jarren Duran 2-11, Caleb Durbin 2-9, Ceddanne Rafaela 4-11, Adley Rutschman 1-6, Nick Sogard 0-3, Trevor Story 0-3
Yankees vs. Tolle: Cody Bellinger 0-3, José Caballero 0-4, Jazz Chisholm Jr. 1-5, Paul Goldschmidt 0-3, Spencer Jones 1-2, Ben Rice 1-3, Amed Rosario 1-6, Ali Sánchez 0-2, Anthony Volpe 0-2, Austin Wells 0-2
Click to refresh | Read more Red Sox stories
By Peter Abraham and Alex Speier
Cam Schlittler owns the Red Sox. That’s the story so far. He has retired nine of 10, six by strikeout. The Sox look overmatched against him once again.
How do you dominate a team that you’ve faced several times? Change looks. Schlittler has thrown 14 curveballs (27 percent usage) through three innings tonight. He didn’t throw more than 19 in any start this year.
By Tim Healey and Cam Kerry
The Red Sox go down in order again. Trevor Story fanned at curveball below the knees, Caleb Durbin dribbled a grounder to second base, and Roman Anthony went down swinging again.
The Red Sox’ only hit through three innings against Cam Schlittler is Adley Rutschman’s bloop single in the first inning. Schlittler’s lifetime ERA against the Red Sox: 0.51.
Anthony has swung and missed four times in two at-bats. He struck out both times trying to check his swing.
By Tim Healey and Alex Speier
Payton Tolle is at 44 pitches through two innings. The Red Sox might be in an awkward spot if he doesn’t get deep into this game. You know Garrett Whitlock has the eighth, Aroldis Chapman the ninth. If the Sox need a particularly long bridge for that gap, how to fill it? Without Justin Slaten and without Tyron Guerrero, the likes of Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Alec Gamboa are important.
Tolle’s velocity took a notable downward turn in the second inning. His four-seamer went from 97.4 m.p.h. in the first to 95.6 m.p.h. in the second; his sinker dropped from 95.9 to 93.7. He’s done that in other starts while working to re-establish command over power, but — another thing worth monitoring as his outing continues.
Payton Tolle gets out of the jam, stranding two after getting Paul Goldschmidt to bounce out to Caleb Durbin at third base.
By Peter Abraham and Alex Speier
The Yankees break through first, with three hits in the second inning. A two-out, run-scoring single by Austin Wells scores George Lombard Jr. (the second youngest Yankee ever with a postseason hit, behind only Mickey Mantle) from second. The throw from Wilyer Abreu to the plate was uncharacteristically far off the mark — based on how hard Wells hit the ball, it seemed like Abreu would have a shot at cutting down Lombard Jr. at the plate.
By Peter Abraham, Cam Kerry, and Alex Speier
Cam Schlittler sets down Ceddanne Rafaela, Nick Sogard, and Jarren Duran in order to close out a strong inning from the Yankees ace.
In the top of the second, Rafaela looked like he was moving with a bit of discomfort both running to first on a slow infield grounder to third and while jogging deliberately back to the dugout. He remains in the game but given his recent quad injury and hamstring cramping, it’s a situation worth monitoring.
He’s thrown 37 pitches through two  innings — his fifth most pitches through two innings this year. Schlittler has retired six of seven, four by strikeout. He has faced the Sox six times (regular season and postseason, counting tonight) and has allowed two earned runs over 34 1/3 innings — an 0.52 ERA.
By Cam Kerry and Alex Speier
Payton Tolle skirts arounds a double off the bat of Ben Rice, stranding the Cohasset native at second base to keep a scoreless inning. Tolle induced a fly out from Paul Goldschmidt before the Rice double, then fanned Heliot Ramos and got Cody Bellinger to line out to second base. He threw 20 pitches in the frame.
Tolle came out throwing heat, touching 99.2 mph against Ben Rice (the fastest pitch Tolle has thrown this year was 99.5 mph), but then — after Rice’s double — dialed back a bit from the stretch.
As he walked off the mound, Tolle — with a grin — pointed to the sky and then pantomimed pushing down towards the ground with both hands. Perhaps a sign that he had now had a chance to steady some nerves?
By Peter Abraham, Cam Kerry, and Alex Speier
Cam Schlittler struck out three, surrendering just a single to Adley Rutschman to get out of the first inning.
Schlittler featured nuclear stuff in the first inning, unloading both his four-seamer and sinker at up to 101 m.p.h. while also mixing in a few wipeout curveballs. Schlittler threw five curveballs in the inning — his most in the first inning of any outing this year. While Schlittler struck out three batters, Rutschman helped force him to throw 22 pitches in the first inning. Rutschman had a broken bat single on the 10th pitch of a very impressive at-bat against Schlittler. It was just the seventh at-bat of 10-plus pitches this year against Schlittler, and the first since Aug. 3.
Schlittler has 15 strikeouts in nine postseason innings against the Red Sox, and 42 in 33 1/3 innings overall.,
What version of Willson Contreras are the Red Sox going to get? He has two at-bats in the 12 days since getting hit in the right hand with a pitch.
In his first at-bat against Cam Schlittler, he struck out swinging at three consecutive pitches.
To the naked eye, he also seemed not nearly as on top of the plate as he usually is. Contreras likes to get in the heads up opposing pitchers by crowding the plate, really getting up near that inside chalk of the batter’s box. That is one reason he gets hit so often -- including two weeks ago in Texas. Tonight, he seemed backed up a bit.
10-pitch at-bat results in a bloop single for Adley Rutschman. Only his third hit in 21 career postseason at-bats.
Yankees starter Cam Schlittler pumps in a 101 m.p.h. fastball to Roman Anthony on the game’s first pitch.
Noted Red Sox draftee Tino Martinez threw out the ceremonial first pitch. Martinez was taken by the Sox in the third round of the 1985 draft but didn’t sign. He was taken by the Mariners in the 1st round in 1988, spent six years with them, then was traded to the Yankees prior to the 1996 season, thus positioning him to be part of the Yankees’ four titles from 1996-2000.
Chad Tracy went to home plate for the lineup card exchange. The Yankees delegated the responsibility to bench coach Luis Rojas.
During player introductions, members of the Red Sox starting lineup are being showered with boos — as expected. Willson Contreras, much as he did at the Home Run Derby this year in Philadelphia, cupped both of his ears to egg on the crowd.

articles.title_orig: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.content_orig:
Caleb Flynn, a former "American Idol" contestant and pastor, has been found guilty of murder in the killing of his wife , Ashley Flynn, after he tried to pin the blame on an intruder breaking into his home in February.
Flynn was found guilty of nine charges in total, including aggravated murder and three charges of murder, two charges of felonious assault and three charges of tampering with evidence. The jury also found Flynn used a firearm in relation to seven of the charges, which carries a sentencing enhancement to those crimes.
He is set to be sentenced on Oct. 5.
Flynn began tearing up as the guilty verdicts were read in court Tuesday. Afterward, while lawyers from both sides spoke with the judge about possible sentencing dates, Flynn hunched over and appeared to be struggling to hold back further tears.
The jury deliberated for about two hours, which led Flynn's defense attorney to later quip it was "twice the time that the O.J. [Simpson] verdict came back on, for those old enough to remember that."
Prosecutors said Flynn, 40, shot his wife twice in the back of the head while she was asleep in bed on Feb. 16. They alleged he then staged their Tipp City, Ohio, home to mimic a break-in and called 911 to claim an intruder was responsible for the murder. The gun used in the shooting has not been recovered.
Flynn had claimed he was in another room when his wife, 37, was killed.
"Today's verdict brings justice and accountability for Ashley's death, and our family is deeply grateful to everyone who helped bring us to this moment," Ashley's family said in a statement read by prosecutor Paul Watkins after the trial. "However, no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother or erase the pain our family has endured."
Watkins said he was done talking about Flynn and urged the community and the media to focus on Ashley instead.
"This world would be a much better place if all of us in it lived like Ashley," he said.
Flynn's attorney, Patrick Mulligan, told reporters after the verdict was read that Flynn maintains his innocence and, "I fully anticipate that there will be a notice of appeal filed, and this decision will be tested thoroughly in the Court of Appeals."
Asked about Flynn's reaction to being found guilty on all charges, Mulligan said his client was "upset. And I understand that because, I think he had expectations. And, you know, it's disappointing."
In a statement later Tuesday, Mulligan said: "We have deep respect for the jury system in the United States. At the same time, we are disappointed with the results. Not all juries answer questions correctly. I am confident that this decision by the jury will be tested as many times as is required during the appeal process, which will undoubtedly begin after sentencing."
In damning testimony , Alleigha Botner, 24, who had an affair with the defendant, testified over two days about the tens of thousands of text messages the two shared, including some in which he wrote he wanted his wife dead.
Botner testified to a roughly 18-month sexual affair with Flynn, whom she met when she was an intern at his church. She described how the two hid their messages, admitted to lying to the FBI at first, and explained how she lost her phone and work laptop just weeks before Ashley's death.
Asked how she feels about Flynn today, she testified, "I hate him."
In the texts, many of which were read in court, Flynn repeatedly said he wished Ashley was dead.
"I need her to die, to cheat again, to leave," Flynn wrote to Botner about his wife on Feb. 11, 2025, almost exactly a year before she was shot. Weeks later, he texted Botner, "I hate her as well and I want her gone." On March 24, 2025, Botner wrote, "What can I do?" and he responded, "Kill her."
Flynn once texted Botner, "I was up until 4 a.m. last night ... trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail. If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."
Botner said Flynn talked about leaving Ashley "four or five times" starting around August 2025, and she set deadlines for October, November, December and possibly January.
Botner said she gave him a final deadline of Jan. 11, 2026, to separate from Ashley, then cut off contact until Feb. 14, two days before the murder. During that gap, he sent her a song he wrote, including the line, "Life is now empty since the moment I lost you."
In his last messages to Botner from the night before the killing, Flynn wrote, "It's happening," "actions will come tomorrow," "I choose you" and "about to be free." He also said Feb. 16 would be "a day I never forget" and "Tomorrow is a big day." Botner told the court she understood "actions" to mean the divorce.
Flynn's lawyers said he was asleep at the time of the shooting and awoke to gunshots while he was in their daughter Ava's room.
"Caleb is not on trial for being a bad husband," his attorney, Emily Smith, said during opening statements, conceding he had an affair with Botner. "He's not on trial for cheating. ... A man can fail as a husband without being a murderer."
Tipp City police released body camera video of them arriving at the house after Flynn called 911, with video of him crying and asking, "Is she, is she gone, sir?"
Flynn's attorneys argued there was no proof he shot his wife.
FBI Special Agent Sarah Deamron testified on the alleged break-in at the house, saying she found no pry, kick or ram marks on the outside of the door. She found gouge marks on the inside trim of the frame, she said, as opposed to the outside as one would expect. She said she had seen about 75 doors forced open, and the one in this case was not consistent with a forced entry.
FBI Special Agent Andrea Kinzig, who testified during the trial, said she found no evidence on Ashley's phone of her having an affair as Flynn had told Botner, according to her testimony.
Flynn did not take the stand.
"You heard his statement three times with the police. There wasn't any reason to put him on for a fourth time," Mulligan said after the trial of the decision not to have Flynn testify.
While text messages were recovered from Caleb and Ashley Flynn's phones, none were able to be taken from Botner's devices. She said on the stand her phone had fallen into the water on a solo trip to Clearwater, Florida, and stopped working. Her laptop, meanwhile, she said was lost on a flight on the way home and never recovered.
"I genuinely ... it was completely innocent ... anyone who knows me knows that I lose things," she told the court.
Flynn's defense lawyers argue Botner's phone and computer being lost is not a coincidence and suggest it could mean she played a role in the murder. However, Ring video shown during the trial showed she was at home during the time the murder was committed.
In her first interview with FBI agents, Botner told them she did not believe that Flynn had killed his wife, but in her second interview with agents, she said she did, ultimately concluding her death was "way too much of a coincidence," she testified in court.
Botner was not charged in the case, and told the court she was not offered anything for her testimony. She told the court when she texted she wanted Ashley "gone," she meant divorce.
The defense called no witnesses in the trial.
Caleb Flynn appeared on season 12 of "American Idol," which took place in 2013. He was given a "golden ticket" to Hollywood after auditioning but was cut early on in the competition.
"Music is all I know, it's what I live to do and I love to sing, so that's why I auditioned," he said in videos from the show. "Maybe my wife kinda nudged me a little too."
He also raved about Ashley, adding Carrie Underwood was his favorite contestant and his wife would look just like her if she dyed her hair blond.
"I love my wife more than anything. She is very, very pretty," he said. "I love her."
In closing arguments Tuesday, Miami County Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins picked apart each of Flynn's defenses.

articles.title_orig: Trump signs executive order renaming AI to ‘super intelligence’
articles.title_zh: Trump signs executive order renaming AI to ‘super intelligence’
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.

A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

articles.title_orig: Immigrant shot by ICE in Austin is charged with assault by Justice Department
articles.title_zh: Immigrant shot by ICE in Austin is charged with assault by Justice Department
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors in Texas announced charges on Tuesday against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , a Venezuelan delivery driver shot and seriously wounded by an ICE officer in Austin earlier this month. The charges came a day before he was set to appear in court to challenge the legality of his immigration detention.
Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.
Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer in the upper part of his back on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries. His attorneys say the bullet is still lodged near his spine, causing “grave danger.” A Democratic congressman who visited Garcés last week said he was in a wheelchair, in pain and in need of surgery.
“We are all laser-focused on making sure that Wilber doesn’t die in custody,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the legal nonprofit Texas Civil Rights Project who is part of Garcés’ legal team .
Garcés Pérez had his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday, said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons in a statement .
The criminal complaint accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an ICE officer’s torso with his car’s side mirror while trying to drive away. This officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the encounter, as the Department of Homeland Security has stated previously, but the complaint includes images appearing to capture this moment from the body camera of a second ICE officer who was also there. After this, “a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area” ensued, the complaint states.
Tuesday’s court appearance following the criminal complaint took Garcés Pérez’s legal team “as a surprise,” they told NBC News in a statement.
“His attorneys only learned of this appearance due to a pre-scheduled meeting they had with him this morning, in which he did not appear,” their statement said. “This morning, when his attorneys were finally able to see him, he was in considerable pain, dizzy, and needed pain medication, which had not been provided. Rather than provide the life saving medical care he needs, DHS and the government are playing games with his life.”
Garcés Pérez was transferred out of a facility in San Antonio, where he had been in immigration custody for nine days, and placed in federal criminal custody in a facility near Austin, according to Garza.
“It has created a web of detention for him,” she said of having Garcés Pérez be transferred from custody.
According to the complaint, after the chase began, the ICE officer wearing his body camera — identified in the complaint by the initials D.F. — lost sight of Garcés Pérez and of the other ICE officer, who was not wearing his body camera and is identified in the complaint by the initials L.G.
The ICE officer who was not wearing his body camera eventually called his colleague. “L.G. told D.F. that Garcs had attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the complaint states. The complaint provides no visual evidence of that interaction.
The complaint also includes the account of events Garcés Pérez provided to federal investigators. He said an SUV from one of the ICE officers struck his “car and caused it to spin around” following a short pursuit, the complaint states. “After coming to a forced stop, Garces recalled L.G. firing his pistol into the backright window of Garces’ car. Garces was struck with a bullet in his upper back.”
By contrast, U.S. Attorney Simmons said in the statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol.”
The court hearing scheduled for Wednesday in Garcés Pérez’s lawsuit challenging his detention was canceled.
Last Tuesday, a federal judge had granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to one of his attorneys, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
“We are still fighting to ensure that the government doesn’t re detain him under immigration custody following whatever is being done on the criminal side,” Garza said.
Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.
Nicole Duarte is an assignment editor in NBC News’ Miami bureau.

The authorities alerted the public to the possible danger of an estuarine crocodile (non-AI file photo)
Police in Singapore have charged a man who is accused of posting an AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile in a popular reservoir.
Ye Lin was charged with communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice for allegedly deleting the picture and the application he used.
The fake image caused public concern, authorities allege. The national water agency suspended its work at the city-state's largest reservoir for two days last month after receiving information that a crocodile had been spotted.
Ye Lin, who is from Myanmar, told the court through an interpreter that he intended to plead guilty, according to local media reports.
The Pandan Reservoir is a popular jogging and kayaking spot west of the city centre
The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities.
But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police.
The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty.
In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; Â£5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both.
Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague.
"The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said.
It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.title_zh: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.
Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.
OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.
Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.
“People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session.
The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility.
“People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots.
Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post .
The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users.
“The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI.
Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely.
“To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.”
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement.
OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut.
Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations.
“We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.”
Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI.
OpenAI also unveiled a new model , GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.”
While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.”
Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides.
Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years.
“My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.

articles.title_zh: White Sox vs. Astros live updates, news, starting pitchers for Game 1: Hagen Smith, AJ Blubaugh take the mound to open wild card
articles.content_orig:
The Chicago White Sox return to the postseason after three consecutive 100-loss seasons, including losing a record 121 games in 2024 . This year, they led the AL Central for much of the season before faltering over the final two weeks.
Opposing them in the wild-card round will be the Houston Astros , the first MLB team ever to win a division without a winning record , finishing the season 81-81. The Astros won three of their final four games to seize the AL West but limped into the postseason with an 11-13 record in September.
Both teams will pitch bullpen games in Game 1. Hagen Smith will open for the White Sox. Called up in early August, Smith compiled a 1.29 ERA in 18 appearances with 41 strikeouts in 28 innings. Notably, that ERA jumped to 3.38 on the road this season. RHP AJ Blubaugh gets the nod for Houston. He pitched in 64 games, recording a 3.66 ERA with 94 strikeouts in 96 innings.
White Sox-Astros start time: 5 p.m. ET Location: Daikin Park | Houston TV channel/live stream: Peacock/NBC Sports Network
Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the Houston Astros host the Chicago White Sox in Game 1 of the AL wild-card round.
After three shutout innings from opener Hagen Smith, the White Sox turned to reliever Jordan Hicks in the fourth.
Hicks pitched a 1-2-3 frame including a strikeout of Yainer Diaz to maintain Chicago's 4-0 lead through four innings.
TheWhite Sox received some fan mail that landed differently ahead of today's game.
Hours before their playoff opener against the Astros, the club received a letter from their most famous fan, Chicago native Pope Leo XIV. They soon shared the letter with their fans on social media.
Addressed to team owner Jerry Reinsdorf and dated Sept. 9, the letter doesn't specifically address the playoffs, but rather thanks Reinsdorf for a letter he sent the previous month, extolls the value of sports as a bridge-builder and invokes "the Almighty's abundant blessings" upon Reinsdorf and his loved ones.
Miguel Ullola couldn't make it seven straight outs.
Colson Montomgery hit a leadoff home run off the Astros reliever to extend Chicago's lead to 4-0 in the top of the fourth inning. Ullola got out of the rest of the frame unscathed, but Houston's hole is deeper through 3 ½ innings.
Cam Smith reached first base on a leadoff walk, then made it to third on a sacrifice bunt and a lineout.
But presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez couldn't bring him home. A ground ball to third ended the third inning, and Chicago maintains a 3-0 lead.
Rookie opener Hagen Smith has done his job with three scoreless innings for the White Sox. His day's likely done after 38 pitches (28 for strikes), 2 hits, 1 strikeout and no walks.
Miguel Ullola has now retired six consecutive White Sox batters since taking over with the bases loaded and no outs in the second.
He pitched a 1-2-3 third and has three strikeouts in two innings. More good news for Houston: Ullola's pitch count is only 16. If he keeps this up, he might be able to offer some extended work.
Chicago maintains a 3-0 lead in the middle of the third.
Unlike Houston's, Chicago's bullpen game is off to an optimal start.
Rookie reliever Hagen Smith pitched a 1-2-3 bottom of the second and has retired six of the seven batters he's faced. He's up to 27 pitches (20 strikes) and the White Sox hold a 3-0 lead after two innings.
The bullpen game is not going well for Houston.
Houston reliever Bryan King loaded the bases with two singles and a hit-by-pitch in the top of the second, setting Sam Antonacci up for a two-run single. That extended Chicago's lead to 3-0.
King then allowed a single to Kyle Teel to load the bases again. And he hadn't recorded an out in the frame. Houston's going to its third pitcher of the game with a 3-0 deficit and no outs in the top of the second. Miguel Ullola takes over on the mound to try to stop the bleeding.
It was a cleaner start for White Sox opener Hagen Smith.
He allowed a two-out single to Isaac Paredes, but didn't allow another baserunner in a scoreless top of the first in a 10-pitch frame. Chicago takes a 1-0 lead into the second inning.
It was a rough start for Astros opener AJ Blubaugh, who didn't get out of the first inning.
White Sox leadoff hitter Sam Antonacci reached on an eight-pitch walk, then advanced to third on a throwing error by first baseman Christian Walker on a ground ball. A one-out sac fly by Munetaka Murakami sent Antonacci home for a 1-0 White Sox lead.
Blubaugh then walked Andrew Benintendi on five pitches for his third free pass of the frame, and his day was done.
Blubaugh finishes his day with 3 walks, 0 strikeouts and 1 run (unearned) in 2/3 of an innning. He threw 27 pitches, just 13 of them for strikes.
Bryan King replaced him on the mound to get out of the inning with no further damage and Chicago holding a 1-0 lead.
The White Sox and Astros are up next, and both teams are taking an unorthodox approach.
Both teams are planning to run a bullpen game on the mound. Rookie reliever Hagen Smith is getting the start for the White Sox. The Astros plan to counter with second-year reliever AJ Blubaugh as their opener.
For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past . Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason.
But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday .
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
The Nos. 1 and 2 seeds in each league go to the division winners with the two best records, earning those teams a bye through the wild-card round and home-field advantage in the division series. The Rays (No. 1) and Guardians (No. 2) claimed those seeds in the American League.
The No. 3 seeds go to the third division winners (that's the Astros in the AL), and those teams will host three-game wild-card series against the No. 6 seeds (the White Sox ).
The top wild-card team in each league (the Yankees in the AL) earns the No. 4 seed and will host the No. 5 seed (the Red Sox ) in the wild-card round.
The higher seed also gets home-field advantage in the league championship series, once we get that far.

articles.title_zh: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order , external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

By GREG HEFFER, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:03 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 12:39 EDT, 29 September 2026
Andy Burnham today vowed to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections.
In his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham promised to introduce a 'new politics' through electoral reform.
He confirmed he would fight the next General Election, scheduled for 2029, with a Labour manifesto commitment to alter the system for choosing UK governments.
The PM, a long-time supporter of proportional representation, said a change would ensure 'everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard'.
Mr Burnham announced the creation of a new 'national commission' for electoral reform and invited rival political parties to be part of its work.
Changing the first-past-the-post system to proportional representation could allow smaller parties – including the Greens – to form part of a Westminster government.
Mr Burnham's plans are likely to revive warnings of a 'coalition of chaos' – made up of a variety of Left-wing or nationalist parties – taking charge of Britain.
But in his conference speech in Liverpool, the PM suggested it was the current first-past-the-post system that was to blame for the country's recent churn of premiers.
Andy Burnham today set out his intent to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections
He argued that Britain should not be governed by a 'divisive' administration elected with '30 per cent of the vote or less'.
Just ten weeks on from his brutal ousting of Sir Keir Starmer as PM, Mr Burnham told Labour members there was a need to change the country's politics.
He said: 'Westminster prizes point-scoring over problem-solving. And that is why so many things go unfixed for so long.
'If we want to change Britain, we need to change ourselves. I will work as hard as I can to get as much cross-party support for our plan for Britain as I can.
'If we can secure that, it will project a message of confidence and stability to the markets and the world about Britain's future direction.'
The PM has so far refused to call a snap General Election in order to win his own mandate from the country.
This is despite him having called for the Tories to do exactly that when they changed leaders while in power.
But he used his first Labour conference speech as PM to demand a 'new politics', as he bowed to calls from his party's MPs for a national commission on electoral reform.
Mr Burnham added: 'We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times.
'It is always in my mind that I'm the seventh PM in ten years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
'We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No10 to a divisive government on 30 per cent of the vote or less.
'Conference, in past years you have voted twice to support electoral reform.
'I hear you, I agree with you and today I am announcing a new national commission on electoral reform.
'I invite all political parties to be a part of its work.
'We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard.'
However, immediately after Mr Burnham's speech, senior Labour figures questioned his desire to pursue a change to the UK's voting system.
Asked if there were any elements of the speech she may not have agreed on, skills minister Jacqui Smith, said: 'Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities.
'Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested with what it comes out with.
'But you know, respect to Andy, he has also long argued for that – it is something that has got a lot of support in the hall, probably a considerable amount of support in the country, and fair enough to him for trying to find a way through it.'
Former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn described Mr Burnham's address as an 'inspirational speech' but also suggested he was unsure about electoral reform.
'We'll see what the commission on electoral reform produces,' he said.
Labour's party conference voted to support moving towards a proportional representation voting system in 2022.
But the party's 2024 manifesto instead focused its electoral and constitutional changes on extending voting to 16 and 17-year-olds and House of Lords reform.
Mr Burnham has previously spoken of how his late father Roy – who died earlier this month after suffering with Alzheimer's – was unaware that his son had swung behind one of his political passions, a change in the voting system to proportional representation.
'I don't think he's ever realised, because of his condition, that I've come round to PR, which is one of his missions – to get me to accept that,' the PM told The Times in July.

OpenAI held its annual DevDay developer conference on Tuesday, where the artificial intelligence company announced a flurry of new products and features .
This year's DevDay comes as OpenAI has been under intense pressure to address mounting safety concerns after it disclosed several incidents where its models behaved in unintended ways, and the startup held back its latest Astra model over safety concerns.

CNBC's reporters are covering the OpenAI DevDay event live from San Francisco, and remotely from Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey.
Friar said OpenAI wants to IPO "when the time is right for our business," echoing Altman's earlier comments to CNBC. She said an IPO is "not a destination," but a "milestone on the journey" and "another type of fundraising."
"I think Sam is correct in saying we don't want to get distracted by suddenly being a public company in the midst of really making sure we drive home for customers our focus on safety and alignment," Friar said.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar touted the company's latest price drop on their GPT-6.1 Sol model, and went deeper into the feedback OpenAI's been getting on their higher pricing tiers.
"When we launched our $200 SKU, people thought we'd lost our minds, [that] no one's ever going to spend that per month," Friar told CNBC's Kate Rooney in an interview.
"What we see is not only are people willing to spend more, they're actually moving more towards consumption in consumer, so not just seat-based pricing, but actually saying, 'I need to consume even more credits because I'm getting this great outcome for maybe my small business,'" she added.
Friar said OpenAI has had an "incredible" third quarter. She confirmed CNBC's earlier reporting that the company has seen 70% quarter over quarter growth, and that its enterprise business has doubled since July.
She added that OpenAI's consumer business has benefitted from a number of factors, including better models, images, voice, and the back to school and work period in the U.S. and around the world.
"People are starting to see us show up the ways they need us to show up," Friar said.
Friar declined to comment on whether OpenAI is engaging in early-stage fundraising discussions with investors, as CNBC reported earlier on Tuesday. She emphasized that OpenAI raised $122 billion in March, and said that the company is "very well capitalized."
"My job as a CFO is always to make sure we're making the right decisions on when we take in more capital and then how we deploy that capital," Friar said.
Friar said OpenAI is being more vocal about safety because of what has been happening "out there in the world." But she noted that while there are instances where OpenAI will hold back, there are also instances where the company will continue to "show model progression."
"When we have to pace the frontier, we'll do that," Friar said. "That's what we're showing right now."
Friar told CNBC that the new Dots AI agents that OpenAI announced will help users "have a better day, be more productive, and maybe get home earlier."

OpenAI is engaging in early stage discussions with investors about a potential funding round, CNBC confirmed on Tuesday.

articles.title_zh: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."
Trump and the CEOs said they had signed an "Accord on Super Intelligence" that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."
Some executives on hand said the accord would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.
Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.
"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."
Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.
The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.
"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.
The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart . The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.
After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.
Other notable guests included Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) president Greg Brockman, Palantir ( PLTR ) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon ( AMZN ) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.
The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.
And in Florida, the attorney general unveiled a new state-level challenge asking a court to halt OpenAI's training of new models unless it puts outside safeguards in place.
But that skepticism didn't change the tenor of the gathering in Washington.
Trump repeatedly brushed off worries about the technology, saying after the meeting that he believes AI will make the world a safer place and that fears about data centers driving up costs were overblown.
He said instead that these new facilities "are going to make communities very happy."
At an event earlier in the day to launch a new government website powered by AI, Trump promised that AI is "going to mostly be put to great use and we'll stop the bad use," through the Department of Justice and FBI.
He added he would "never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."

articles.title_orig: Riley's homer rallies Braves past Phillies in wild-card opener
articles.title_zh: Riley's homer rallies Braves past Phillies in wild-card opener
articles.content_orig:
The Phillies lost to the Braves , 5-3, in Game 1 of the best-of-three Wild Card Series Tuesday afternoon in Atlanta. The Phillies took a 3-2 lead in the top of the seventh inning on a two-RBI triple from catcher J.T. Realmuto before manager Don Mattingly decided to hand the ball over to his closer, Jhoan Duran .
Duran was one of the best closers in baseball in the regular season, but seeing him enter the game in the seventh inning was still a surprising move. He hadn't worked in the seventh inning all season and only did twice (once in the regular season, once in the playoffs) last year. He's generally a ninth-inning-only closer but has gotten some four-out saves.
In this situation, the Braves had the top of the order coming up in the top of the seventh (it was 9-1-2 to start).
"We talked about it before the game: if we were at the top, we were getting to the top, go seventh, eighth (innings)," Mattingly said after the game.
Duran only threw 11 pitches in the seventh inning, then got two outs in the bottom of the eighth before a weak tapper from Michael Harris II turned into an infield single. Duran then hit Ozzie Albies with a pitch before Austin Riley hit a three-run home run. That 3-2 lead turned into a 5-3 deficit that would hold for a final score.
There's an argument that Duran should've been removed before Riley hit, given that the closer was up over 20 pitches at this point -- but there were two outs and he's the best reliever the Phillies have. The Harris hit was only 85.5 mph, just a bouncer that was placed perfectly in the infield.
Mattingly noted after the game that had Duran gotten through the seventh and eighth with a tidy pitch count, he'd have checked with his closer and possibly sent him back out for the ninth. It was a case where the Phillies were trying to use their best and see how deep he could get.
Had the Phillies used a lesser reliever and blown the game, there would've been questions about why one of the top relievers on the planet was sitting in the bullpen unused. Instead of managing to the save stat, Mattingly put his best guy in position to get the game to the ninth with the lead intact. The next question would be who was going to get the ninth inning. If you don't get there with the lead, it doesn't much matter. Saving the best reliever often backfires in the postseason. We've famously seen shots of stud closers like Zach Britton and Craig Kimbrel helplessly watching as their team blew the lead. This time around, Mattingly and the Phillies made the right call. It just didn't work out.
"It's frustrating," Mattingly said. "But in our minds, we had our best guy out there. You live with this one."
Sometimes even the best plans backfire.

articles.title_orig: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.title_zh: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.content_orig:
His slam dunk was a brick.
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., accused former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday of committing perjury when he denied having attended a specific Atlanta Hawks basketball game in 2024 — to Smith’s apparent confusion.
The attempted trick play happened during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Smith’s now-scuttled investigations into President Donald Trump. But it soon emerged that Schmitt had the wrong team.
“Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on Feb. 3, 2024?” Schmitt asked.
“What city would that be in?” a confused-looking Smith replied.
“Atlanta,” Schmitt responded.
Schmitt pressed him again about whether he was in Atlanta on that date and then said he’d give him some “context” — it was the day after Fani Willis , the district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia, “came clean” about her romantic relationship with a prosecutor in her then-pending criminal case against Trump.
“The next day were you in Atlanta?” Schmitt continued.
“I do not believe so,” Smith responded. “I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”
Schmitt then asked whether he ever met with the local prosecutors in Atlanta who charged Trump. “No,” Smith said.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta, at a Warrior-Hawks game, on Feb. 3, 2024, the day after Willis and [Nathan] Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt continued as a staffer held up a poster board that had three text messages about Smith’s going to an event.
The staffer quickly took the poster down as Smith looked on, appearing confused.
“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Schmitt said.
Smith complained that it had been taken down too quickly and that he hadn’t gotten to look at it. “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” Schmitt told him, adding later that he’d go down in history as “a total dirtbag.”
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who was next in line to question Smith, gave him an opportunity to further respond to Schmitt’s attack.
Smith said the only game he remembered going to around that time was a University of Maryland basketball game against the Iowa Hawkeyes featuring star player Caitlin Clark. “The Marshals Service was there with me. You could check if that was the exact date,” Smith said.
Klobuchar then checked the date of the Maryland-Iowa game.
“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93-85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over, scored 30 points,” and the game was in Maryland, she said.
She also chided Schmitt for appearing to mix up the Hawks and the Hawkeyes.
“I would just say for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said.
Schmitt didn’t apologize. Asked by NBC News afterward whether he still thought Smith had perjured himself, he said: “We’ll find out. That’s going to be up to a prosecutor to determine. My job here today was to ask questions and get answers.”
Despite the flub, some right-wing commentators and outlets praised Schmitt for the exchange. Pro-Trump influencer Benny Johnson posted on X that Schmitt “CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself” and “pulled out the receipts.” The post appeared to have been taken down by the late afternoon.
Schmitt later went on “ The Charlie Kirk Show ,” where one of the hosts praised him for the “great moment.” “Good for you on that,” host Andrew Kolvet said.
“Gotta give you some flowers for that, sir,” he said, saying Smith “sat there acting dumbfounded and completely clueless.”
“It was the only NBA or NCAA men’s game going on at that time in Atlanta. He claimed later that he was at another game,” Schmitt responded. “Here’s the thing — my job is to ask the questions. If that’s what his answer is, that’s what his answer is.”
On Tuesday night, Schmitt wrote in a post on X , “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”
Rebecca Shabad is a politics reporter for NBC News based in Washington.
