Warner Bros. is asking moviegoers to “decide for yourself” with a new ad for Tom Cruise’s “ Digger ” that touts both negative and positive reactions.
“Masterpiece” and “Unpleasant” are quoted in the same still of the new trailer, which also toggles between the words “Brilliant” and “Baffling” as well as “Magnificent” and “Insufferable.” These quotes are from film influencers who screened the movie early and posted their reactions after the social embargo lifted on Sept. 22.
“Same film, different truth,” reads the ad for “Digger,” which stars Cruise as an oil tycoon whose drilling triggers a climate crisis. The film, from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, marks Cruise’s first non-action hero role in nearly a decade.
Warner Bros. posted the new ad an hour before the review embargo, which is when film critics were allowed to publish their reviews. The “decide for yourself” campaign may have been an attempt to get ahead of the critics, who were, as a whole, far less generous than the first wave of social media pundits.
Variety ‘s Owen Gleiberman called the film “so full of itself” in his review , writing, “The movie cost north of $125 million to make, and that figure is not only too big to probably justify itself; it’s a testament to the arrogance of the filmmakers — to the assumption that we’ll turn out in droves for this ponderous absurdist lecture.”
Bilge Ebiri of Vulture wrote in his review, “‘Digger’ is a torturous experience, sometimes purposefully so, often unintentionally so.” And David Ehrlich of IndieWire dubbed it a “surreal misfire,” giving the movie a C+ grade. (“Digger” currently sits at a 52% score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes.)
Of course, those are just critics’ opinions, so for those waiting to decide for themselves, “Digger” premieres in theaters on Oct. 2.

The yields on longer-dated U.S. Treasurys rose Tuesday, adding to their rip-roaring moves to multi-year highs due to concerns around inflation and central bank monetary policy.
The 30-year Treasury bond yield, which typically reacts to geopolitical developments, was more than 2 basis points higher at 5.585%. Earlier in the session, it jumped to just above 5.6%, or its highest level since June 2002 when the long-dated bond yield hit 5.644%. The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — traded about 1 basis point higher at 5.253%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which tends to move in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, fell more than 3 basis points to 4.891%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
"Investors remain very focused on inflation and they're more worried about the fiscal deficits here in the U.S... [as well as] the amount of Treasury supply," JoAnne Bianco, senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management, told CNBC. "All of those things make them think there needs to be more term premium."
The recent spike in borrowing costs, which has seen yields move to multiyear highs, comes as the U.S. and Iran held separate talks with mediators with the aim of resolving the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, according to a report by Al Jazeera.
The seven-month war continues to weigh on energy prices, fueling investor expectations of further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve to help tackle runaway price increases, which have been exacerbated by rising government debt.
Traders are now pricing in a more than 72% chance of another Fed rate hike at its next meeting in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That comes after the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee earlier this month voted by 12-0 to raise its main interest rate by 25 basis points.

articles.title_zh: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
articles.content_orig:
Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.
One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday.
Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.
Ramancha remains at large.
Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk.
The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said.
The newly unsealed indictment says that in July 2023, Ramancha executed a sales and purchase agreement with an unidentified company in Lakeland, Florida, agreeing to supply that company with a product described as being Ozempic "at deeply discounted pricing."
A month later, Ramancha executed another agreement with a company in Sanford, Florida, to supply it with a product described as "Ozempic syringes" at deeply discounted pricing, the indictment alleges.
in November 2023, "Roy utilized threats to facilitate the distribution of product in the United States," writing, "Listen i am not your friend okay? I am not that guy," the indictment alleges.
Roy continued, "I am the guy that will cut some one [expletive] head off and [expletive] peoples dead wives corpse with it," the indictment alleges. "You [expletive] up Solve the [expletive] problem. Get the truck over there today."
After Roy and Ramancha learned that the FDA had seized some of their product that they had distributed in the U.S., a co-conspirator asked Ramancha whether the related FDA warning would affect a pending order to 60,000 additional units of Ozempic, the indictment says.
"Ramancha replied, 'Not at all. But you have to make sure your client are not being idiotic,'" the indictment alleges.
The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S.
In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in  2026, compared to 3% in 2024.
"And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted.
"Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday.
"These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has personally driven the controversial, taxpayer-funded video ads promoting himself and his administration’s policies, including helping select the imagery and videos used, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.
Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging.
Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.
“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters in the Capitol on Monday.
GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas echoed that sentiment: “It’s not even a close question.”
The White House has broadly defended the ads, saying they are akin to public service announcements past administrations have put out about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations. Officials have insisted they “are very clearly not campaign ads.”
“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said Monday.
But the imagery is undeniably meant to promote Trump, casting him as a warrior battling against existential threats. And the latest one appears nearly identical to a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.
That most recent ad shows Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad , echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.
The version on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text. The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the new version of the ad.
Multiple members of Trump’s political operation said they were unaware that these ads were coming until they aired. But another source pushed back on the notion that anyone was kept in the dark — noting that the president had spoken about the ads to multiple aides and advisers and insisting that they were not being made in secret.
The latest ad — which aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game — is the third government-funded message in recent days to be captured by the media tracker AdImpact.
An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. Text on the screen touted his administration’s accomplishments, including “reigniting American manufacturing.”
“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”
The music used in that ad — a song called “Love Me” by JMSN — has also come under scrutiny. Lawyers for the artist sent White House chief of staff Susie Wiles a letter on Monday asking the administration to “immediately withdraw the advertisement from all scheduled airings” and “cease and desist any use of the Song and/or any of the intellectual property of JMSN.”
A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”
Beyond questions of intellectual property, watchdog groups say the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications.
“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW, in Washington.
GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress,” he said.
And, Sherman noted, the Government Accountability Office — the nonpartisan agency that would be tasked with investigations into this type of issue — is currently without Senate-confirmed leadership.
“That makes it that much harder for them to move with speed to address a high-profile and politically sensitive investigation like this requires,” he said.
Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”
And Raskin, who will gain congressional subpoena power in November if Democrats win the House, said it is not just Trump who might face inquiries over the messages. He said the creation of the ads was a “Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.”
“This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief,” one former Trump campaign official told CNN. “These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.”
The story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The Futuristic-Looking Hyundai Ioniq V Launches At Just $14,800 In China
articles.title_zh: The Futuristic-Looking Hyundai Ioniq V Launches At Just $14,800 In China
articles.content_orig:
Hyundai is on a roll. Around the world, the brand has a series of stylish EV models on sale at affordable prices. Perhaps the grass is greener on the other side, but I often find myself frustrated at the fact that there are so many cool Hyundai EVs that we won’t ever get in the U.S. Case in point: the Hyundai Ioniq V .
When the car was revealed this year at the Beijing Auto show, its Prius-meets-Lamborghini styling stood out, even in a room of hyper-advanced Chinese models. And maybe that was the point. Hyundai's new strategy to turn around its China business starts with the Ioniq V, the first of a series of cars developed in China, for that market. Now it's on sale.
On Tuesday, Hyundai China officially launched the Ioniq V. At about $14,800, it's cheap—and not just by U.S. standards. Even in China, that's a very competitive price. Now, to be fair, that's a limited-time offer. Without that, the official price is around $16,500.
It's a lot of car for the money, too. The Ioniq V is a midsize car, roughly the same size as the gas-powered Hyundai Sonata. But its pricing is on par with compact or even subcompact EV models from Chinese brands. For example, it costs about as much as the compact BYD Dolphin.
It is powered by either a 188-horsepower or 225-horsepower motor turning the front wheels. The less powerful motor is fed by a CATL-sourced 53.5 kWh LFP battery, good for 335 miles (540 km) of estimated range. The larger motor is fed by a 66.8 kWh LFP battery, good for 404 miles (650 km). These numbers are both according to China’s generous CLTC cycle, so expect these ranges to drop if the Ioniq V ever leaves China. It does use Hyundai’s E-GMP 800-volt platform, but no charging times have been specified yet.
The Ioniq V has a full suite of driver-assistance features developed with China's Momenta. There’s an infotainment screen that takes up much of the Ioniq V’s width, running on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8295P system-on-a-chip. This is fancy stuff for such a cheap car here in the U.S., but it's pretty common in China. While many foreign brands have lagged behind Chinese rivals, Hyundai is clearly trying to beat China at its own game, offering a feature-packed car at a budget price.
At the Beijing Auto Show in April, Hyundai CEO José Muñoz committed to staying in the Chinese market and said the company was "tripling down" on it. With such an aggressive pricing strategy for the Ioniq V—and a car that looks to match homegrown rivals on tech and value—it looks like this brand means business.

articles.content_orig:
Senior Entertainment Reporter
Westeros is ready to conquer the big screen .
Warner Bros. announced Tuesday that Game of Thrones : Aegon’s Conquest is set for theatrical release on June 1, 2029. Owen Harris directs the film that has a script from Beau Willimon , marking the first feature film for the franchise that adapts author George R.R. Martin ‘s A Song of Ice and Fire fantasy book series.
The studio confirmed the title at CinemaCon earlier this year for the movie that centers on King Aegon I Targaryen’s conquest of Westeros. Castmembers have not yet been revealed.
A Game of Thrones movie has been discussed for more than a decade , with talk dating back to 2013, two years after the series adaptation of A Song of Ice and Fire first premiered on HBO . Back then, Game of Thrones series co-creators David Benioff and Dan Weiss pitched network brass on the wildly popular program potentially ending with three feature films. The flagship series aired its finale in May 2019.
HBO has two current Game of Thrones series, with House of the Dragon having aired its third season over the summer, while A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms season two is expected next year.
Harris has directed episodes of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms , with his other television credits including Mrs. Davis and Black Mirror . Willimon created House of Cards and served as a writer on the Star Wars series Andor .
Back in 2015, Martin explained why he had previously turned down opportunities for a Game of Thrones film, given that he didn’t want to have to cut out significant portions of his books. He was also concerned that a movie would mostly focus on a character like Jon Snow or Daenerys Targaryen.
“I didn’t need the money, so I had the power to say the sexiest word in Hollywood: ‘no,'” he told The South Bank Show at the time.

The yields on longer-dated U.S. Treasurys rose Tuesday, adding to their rip-roaring moves to multi-year highs due to concerns around inflation and central bank monetary policy.
The 30-year Treasury bond yield, which typically reacts to geopolitical developments, was more than 2 basis points higher at 5.585%. Earlier in the session, it jumped to just above 5.6%, or its highest level since June 2002 when the long-dated bond yield hit 5.644%. The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — traded about 1 basis point higher at 5.253%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which tends to move in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, fell more than 3 basis points to 4.891%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
"Investors remain very focused on inflation and they're more worried about the fiscal deficits here in the U.S... [as well as] the amount of Treasury supply," JoAnne Bianco, senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management, told CNBC. "All of those things make them think there needs to be more term premium."
The recent spike in borrowing costs, which has seen yields move to multiyear highs, comes as the U.S. and Iran held separate talks with mediators with the aim of resolving the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, according to a report by Al Jazeera.
The seven-month war continues to weigh on energy prices, fueling investor expectations of further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve to help tackle runaway price increases, which have been exacerbated by rising government debt.
Traders are now pricing in a more than 72% chance of another Fed rate hike at its next meeting in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That comes after the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee earlier this month voted by 12-0 to raise its main interest rate by 25 basis points.

articles.title_orig: Dennis Haskins, Mr. Belding on ‘Saved by the Bell,’ Dies at 75
articles.title_zh: Dennis Haskins, Mr. Belding on ‘Saved by the Bell,’ Dies at 75
articles.content_orig:
Dennis Haskins, the actor best known for playing the affable Principal Richard Belding on the hit NBC sitcom “Saved by the Bell,” has died. He was 75.
Haskins’ death was confirmed early Tuesday by his agent. Additional details were not immediately available.
“It’s a tragic loss,” his agent, Jay Schachter, said in a statement. “Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I’m heartbroken.”
“Saved by the Bell,” which ran from 1989 to 1993, centered on the antics of a group of students at the fictitious Bayside High in Southern California. Taking a page from the comedy movie “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off,” the school often appeared to be run more by the teens than their hapless principal. The show was both ridiculed and embraced for its zany plots.
Lark Voorhies, who played Lisa Turtle on the show, paid tribute to Haskins in an Instagram post, saying she was heartbroken.
“Knowing Dennis Haskins for almost 40 years has been one of the truest blessings of my life, which makes losing him hurt so deeply,” she wrote. “We shared so much history together from our earliest days, and through it all, he remained a fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart.”
Haskins was born and raised in Chattanooga, Tennessee. According to a biography posted by the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, he was active in the school’s drama club and helped found a community theater group.
Before his television career, he was a music manager, agent and concert promoter, and his clients included Tom Jones and Gregg Allman, according to his biography on IMDb.
Haskins later went on to have guest roles in “The Twilight Zone” and “Magnum, P.I.” in the 1980s.

Defendant Lindsay Clancy looks at the jury after Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in Clancy's murder trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger via AP hide caption
Lindsay Clancy's lawyer argued Tuesday that there wasn't enough evidence to prove she killed her three children, a striking turn after a lengthy trial that focused more on her mental state than on whether she took their lives.
"This entire case is based on speculation," attorney Kevin Reddington said during the first hearing since Clancy's trial ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury. They were split 11 to 1 in her favor.
During that trial, Reddington didn't dispute that Clancy killed the children at the family's home in 2023. Instead, the defense sought to persuade the jury that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was not criminally responsible because of mental disease, a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. ___

But at Tuesday's hearing, Reddington sought to persuade Judge William Sullivan — the same judge who presided over the first trial — to acquit Clancy.
There is, Reddington contended, not enough evidence "that this woman killed those children." He pointed to matters ranging from her condition when she was found, badly injured and bleeding in the yard outside her home, to her lack of memory of what happened when she woke up in a hospital. At the first trial, her now ex-husband and first responders testified that they arrived at the house and discovered she had tried to kill herself right after killing the children.
"Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this?" Reddington asked, going on to recap his arguments that she also was psychotic and delusional at the time of the children's deaths. He didn't offer any alternative theories or evidence about who might be responsible.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called his argument "laughable," pointing to various evidence raised during the trial. In court papers filed Monday, prosecutors recapped their arguments that there was enough evidence to convict Clancy.
The prosecution maintains that Clancy knew her actions were wrong when she used exercise bands to strangle 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. They said she contrived to get her husband out of the house that evening by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family.
The judge didn't immediately decide, and no trial date was set.
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to retry Clancy, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the hearing. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
"We are going to do what we can for the children," Cruz told reporters outside the court. "That is what this case is about."
Clancy's attorneys have also asked the judge to dismiss the criminal case. Among other things, they have argued that the judge should have ousted the one juror who favored a murder conviction after the jury foreperson complained he was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
The juror, Michael Desronvil, has said through his lawyer that he had no doubts about his stance. Desronvil told Fox News' "Hannity" in a brief video statement on Monday that "the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels," meaning the children.
The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. About a dozen Clancy supporters, most dressed in pink, stood outside court Tuesday waiting for her to arrive.
Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.

articles.title_zh: Tech bull Dan Ives flags 'shocker risk' in Anthropic's IPO leak
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) leaked IPO prospectus had some shocking — perhaps even terrifying — things to say about artificial intelligence.
The company formally warned investors that its technology may pose "existential risks to humanity," according to a report that cited sources with knowledge of the prospectus.
One veteran analyst viewed Anthropic's risk-laden disclosures as creating more headwinds for the industry.
"I continue to view this as kind of a shocker risk relative to what I believe [will happen]," Yorkville Ives partner and longtime tech analyst Dan Ives said on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed . "I do think there's some alarmism that's going on here as well."
The alleged financial results fall under the "shocker" column too.
Anthropic saw its 2025 sales surge 1,088% to $4.59 billion, according to a late Monday report from Reuters , which saw the company's IPO prospectus. An official filing has not been made public yet.

Anthropic lost $41.97 billion last year on a GAAP net basis, up from a loss of $8.31 billion in 2024.
"I think Anthropic is the heart and lungs of the AI revolution," Ives said. "And that goes for OpenAI as well."
"I view it as you are essentially building out a new economy over the next 10 years," he added.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s Dots Are Always-On AI Agents—and Its Answer to Meta’s Muse
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s Dots Are Always-On AI Agents—and Its Answer to Meta’s Muse
articles.content_orig:
Dots are OpenAI’s new always-on AI agents , announced at the company’s DevDay 2026 event on Tuesday in San Francisco. These agents complete tasks on a user’s behalf and are depicted as cute blobs you can personalize and assign multistep projects to complete.
OpenAI’s Dots are powered by the startup’s GPT-6 Astra model . A core selling point is their “always-on” design—unlike a single-turn chatbot experience, these agents constantly crawl the web and attempt to complete whatever task you assign to them. Dots also pull context from connected apps and learn more about your preferences over time.
In one demo example shared by OpenAI, a user’s Dot helps plan dinner. The Dot proactively saw that the user’s calendar showed they were working through dinner and messaged with two GrubHub food delivery options with pricing for each. The user followed up with their food pick and when they wanted it ordered. In another example, a user collaborated with the agent to launch a new website.
Users can message Dots through ChatGPT , Slack, and Microsoft Teams, with the user’s context shared with Dots across modes. In addition, Pro users can join a waitlist to text with their Dots in iMessage or RCS messaging on Android .
The Dots rollout starts today for subscribers to ChatGPT’s Pro tier that costs $100 a month. OpenAI often launches new features first for this higher subscription tier and then rolls them out to a larger subset of users over time. Users can start by controlling one Dot, but the company is expected to eventually roll out the ability to control multiple agents at the same time.
The Dots launch is also part of OpenAI doubling down on its efforts to attract more enterprise clients. On stage at DevDay, CEO Sam Altman announced “specialist Dots” for enterprise customers tuned for specific tasks, like accounting, email marketing, and legal analysis. It adds to the trend of AI agent coworkers being integrated into more professional workflows.
Dots are designed to get explicit approval before taking more sensitive actions on a user's behalf, like installing software or changing a password. Users can enable a Custom Rules tool to set explicit boundaries that they don't want agents to cross, as well as tasks that need more direct permission to complete.
As users connect their data and use agents, it's worth keeping potential security and privacy risks top of mind. OpenAI built safety guardrails into these Dots, but even so, asking agents to automate aspects of your life involves trusting the tools won’t accidentally share information you didn’t intend or get tricked by an online adversary into taking actions you didn’t want. Exercise caution when interacting with this nascent software and connecting data from your pre-existing apps. Also, if your OpenAI account is set to allow model training on your data, this setting carries over to your interactions with the agents.
Personal agents are currently having a breakthrough moment. While this year started with early adopters in Silicon Valley latching onto tools like OpenClaw , the recent release of Meta’s Muse agent reached a larger user base that is now experimenting with personalized agents. Muse rocketed to the top of smartphone app download charts, but Dots has come for Meta's lunch.

articles.title_orig: Trump celebrates Senate passage of legislation to overhaul college sports - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump celebrates Senate passage of legislation to overhaul college sports - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The Senate passed the act with a vote of 77-22 on Monday night.
President Donald Trump celebrated the Senate's passage of the Protect College Sports Act, saying that the legislation will "save college sports" and is a "really big deal."
"This is a really big deal. It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves," Trump wrote in a Monday night social media post.
Trump has long been an advocate for this legislation and said in August that he would sign the bill "immediately" if it came across his desk -- urging both the House and Senate to advance it.
On Monday night, the Senate passed the act with a vote of 77-22, bringing a massive restructuring of college athletics one step closer.
The legislation establishes a federal framework for college athletics to create one set system over the current patchwork of differing state rules. It creates one rulebook on how athletes can earn money from their name, image and likeness (NIL) and puts a cap on the amount of money schools can directly share with their athletes.
But it’s not just about money. The bill also deals with transfers, eligibility and media rights. Athletes can transfer to another school one time without losing a year of eligibility and student-athletes are given five years of eligibility with exceptions for certain circumstances such as a serious injury. The legislation also gives colleges the ability to negotiate broadcasting agreements collectively to give them more control over how their games are marketed and distributed.
Supporters of the bill say that it will add much-needed stability to the world of college athletics that has rapidly changed in recent years due to increasing NIL deals and frequent transfers. Senators -- including Sen. Ted Cruz -- argue that creating one national set of rules will reduce uncertainty and establish clear guidelines for compensation, eligibility and media rights.
"This bill puts an end to the chaos plaguing college athletics. It protects NIL opportunities because student athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent, without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals, it creates clear, enforceable rules for eligibility and transfers. It protects our traditions and rivalries," Cruz said on the Senate floor ahead of Monday's vote.
While the bill received bipartisan support in the Senate on Monday, there were still concerns from many senators, largely around the amount of leverage the bill gives to the NCAA. The NCAA will now be in charge of overseeing school compliance on certain portions of the bill while also being granted immunity from federal antitrust lawsuits when enforcing its rules.
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, one of the bill's opponents, argued that the legislation could give the NCAA greater legal protection and authority without giving athletes an equivalent role in negotiating the rules that govern them.
"You don't need a bill of this sweeping scope to address what are a set of minor but important practices in college athletics that have gotten out of control. We could have either passed a very narrow bill here to address the agent issue and the transfer issue, or we could have done what happens in most industries, which is just say to the NCAA and to the colleges, tough luck. Congress isn't going to come in here and micromanage your relationship with the athletes. If you want to work something out, sit down and talk to the athletes about it," Murphy said.
On Monday night, the NCAA thanked the senators who supported the legislation and looked ahead to the next hurdle: House passage.
"The NCAA thanks the many senators who sponsored this bill -- including Senators Cruz, Cantwell, Schmitt and Coons -- as well as the many other senators who voted for the bill, for their bipartisan effort to protect this uniquely American tradition of college sports in the decades to come," the NCAA wrote in a social media post. "Now the bill moves to the U.S. House of Representatives and there is much work left to do to ensure student-athlete benefits are codified into federal law and future generations of young people can access those benefits and use college sports as the launching point for their careers."
The bipartisan piece of legislation still faces obstacles in the House.
The Congressional Black Caucus has come out against the bill because they believe it doesn't include strong enough protections and economic opportunities for Black athletes. Additionally, some conservative House members have expressed criticism for similar legislation , arguing the government is trying to have too much oversight over college sports.
The House remains out of session for their midterm recess and it is unlikely that they will be called back to Washington early to consider the legislation.
So while the legislation is now in the red zone, it’s going to take more than a "tush push" to get it into the end zone and onto the president's desk.

The Las Vegas Raiders had little business hiring one of the hottest head coaching candidates on the market this past offseason. They were an aimless, unserious franchise that hadn't won a division title since 2002.
But Klint Kubiak, coming off helping the Seattle Seahawks to a Super Bowl title as their offensive coordinator, saw the potential when few did.
"There's just a lot to love about this organization," Kubiak said at his introductory media conference in February, via the team's site . "You look around this building and the resources that we have, our meal room, the weight room, the fields outside, the coaches offices, it's as good as it gets in the NFL. Been in a lot of buildings for good reasons and bad reasons, been hired and fired, and the resources are here. We've just got to go put it all together."
In three games, Kubiak has changed the Raiders. Last season was an absolute mess. The team went 3-14 and barely looked like a professional franchise. That wasn't unusual for the Raiders because they had been a mess for years.
Everything looks different this season. Las Vegas made good, smart decisions in free agency. The Maxx Crosby trade famously didn't work out but that is helping the Raiders this season. They had a plan for top draft pick Fernando Mendoza, to sit him and let Kirk Cousins play. The Raiders look like a competent team on both sides of the ball, with a front office making sharp decisions. It has been decades since that was the case.
The Raiders started 2-0 and it was fine to be skeptical, but a 35-27 win at the Saints might be a turning point . The Raiders forced a turnover on all four Saints possessions in the fourth quarter as they came back to win. The 2025 Raiders probably don't win that game. Neither would the 2024 Raiders, 2023 Raiders, 2022 Raiders or most Raiders teams since Bill Callahan's first season (2002), when they won their last playoff game and reached the Super Bowl.
Las Vegas' defense is second in the NFL in EPA allowed per play, a stunning turnaround from last season. The offense is 16th in EPA per play but two of those games came without Brock Bowers , who reminded everyone Sunday, with 116 yards and a touchdown, that he's the NFL's best tight end. Cousins is running a clean operation and the Kubiak influence on the offense is evident.
This weekend might be the biggest game for the Raiders since they moved to Las Vegas, though the team has been there only since 2020. They host the 3-0 Chiefs on Sunday afternoon. The Raiders have won two of their last five games against the Chiefs (one came against Chris Oladokun at QB, not Patrick Mahomes ), but this matchup is different. There's real hope for the Raiders coming into this meeting, not just a fleeting moment that gets washed away with another long losing streak. The Raiders will go into that game feeling confident they can win.
The Raiders are 3-0. And there are no signs yet that it's a mirage.
Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 3 of the NFL season:
The 1976 Buccaneers are the standard for bad teams in NFL history. They went 0-14 with -287 point differential, which is an NFL record. That's -20.5 per game. The 2026 Dolphins are 0-3 with a point differential of -50, which is -16.7 per game. The Dolphins aren't quite on the '76 Bucs' pace, but they're also not an expansion team.
And now Miami will be without running back De'Von Achane , the most talented player on the roster who suffered a season-ending torn ACL in Week 3. And still, Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley is being optimistic. Miami lost by 14 points on Sunday to the Chiefs, but it was a one-score game until the final three minutes.
"That's why this one hurts," Hafley said, via Local10.com. "It's a four-point game in the third quarter. It's a seven-point game with us driving after we got backed up. We got the penalty to get the ball to the 50. I mean, I felt like we were right there."
Cam Ward 's final pass on Sunday was dispiriting. The Giants didn't score a touchdown, so Tennessee's defense did its job. Finally, in the fourth quarter, the Titans' offense woke up and had the ball inside the 10-yard line with a chance to take a lead in the final minute. And on first down, with two timeouts left, Ward had room to run but instead forced a pass that went right to safety Jevon Holland for an interception. Game over.
"He's out in the open, I'd just be smarter with the football," Titans head coach Robert Saleh said . "We've got two timeouts left, it's first-and-goal at the 8, we're going to score, you don't have to force it in that situation. Unfortunately it happened."
Saleh sounded exacerbated. Saleh was asked if Ward would be benched and he said no, but it has to be a consideration if Ward doesn't improve. Ward is 30th among 34 qualified quarterbacks in adjusted EPA ( expected points added ) per play. Last season, he was 52nd of 60. There hasn't been any tangible progress.
The Buccaneers had to know they were taking a risk in going into the season with undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels as their backup quarterback . Now Daniels is next in line with Baker Mayfield reportedly out two-to-four weeks with a thumb injury. The Buccaneers have Easton Stick on the practice squad, and at least he has four career starts. The Chargers , however, lost all four of those starts.
The Buccaneers are 2-10 in their last 12 games. They have not covered the point spread in 12 straight games, a record in the Super Bowl era . And now an 0-3 team has to somehow maintain with either an undrafted rookie or a practice squad journeyman at quarterback for maybe a month. Head coach Todd Bowles has to be the favorite to be the first head coach fired .
"Funny thing, we're 0-3 and we're a game out of first place," Bowles told the media after Sunday's game, via Pewter Report . "We have to get our stuff together. We got to reach down and do more. To a coach, to a person, or to a player, we've got to do more."
The Chargers' season has been fascinating. Last week, they matched the 1926 Racine Tornadoes by losing their first two games at home by double digits against teams that had a win percentage of less than .200 the previous season. On Sunday, they forced five turnovers, had a +4 turnover margin and still lost to the Bills. Teams posting those turnover numbers have lost only three times since 2013 and, amazingly, all three times the Chargers have been the losing team, according to Evan Abrams of Action Network.
The Chargers had more than enough breaks to beat the Bills and still somehow trailed 24-13 at the two-minute warning. Even if the Chargers don't feel like the fourth-worst team in the NFL, the results say they are.
At least the Cardinals woke up and realized they should be featuring Jeremiyah Love, the third overall pick of the draft. They gave him 21 of 23 running back carries and he had 90 yards. He added five receptions for 19 yards and a touchdown.
"Left a lot out there, I feel like," Love told ESPN . "I feel like I could help the team a lot more."
The Cardinals didn't play poorly against the 49ers , cutting their deficit to one score three different times in the fourth quarter. With that and a win at the Chargers already, the Cardinals might be a tougher out than expected.
The Jets were practically forced to give rookie first-round tight end Kenyon Sadiq (39% of offensive snaps through two games) a bigger role due to injuries to tight end Mason Taylor and receiver Adonai Mitchell . And Sadiq had a big breakout. He had seven catches for 105 yards and a touchdown. The TD was a fantastic catch in the end zone.

articles.title_orig: ‘New path’: UK’s Burnham promises huge expansion of public services
articles.title_zh: ‘New path’: UK’s Burnham promises huge expansion of public services
articles.content_orig:
UK Labour conference tests Andy Burnham’s popularity against economic reality
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to put the United Kingdom on a new path of equitable growth during his first Labour conference speech as leader of the country and party.
Covering a range of topics including healthcare, pensions, electoral reforms, affordable housing and publicly-owned utilities, Burnham on Tuesday said it was time for the UK to opt for drastic change and reject a slow and painful demise.
“Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time,” Burnham told delegates, adding that he was “ready to do things my predecessors wouldn’t”.
“I will make a break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path, build a new economy and a new politics. That is the case I make to you today,” he said.
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as the UK prime minister in July, said there was a “sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”.
“More of the same isn’t good enough,” said the former mayor of Manchester, where the party conference was held. He added that it was time “to break the mould today”.
This year’s Labour Party conference brought together legislators and party members alongside trade unions and businesses in one place.
“This country isn’t where any of us would want it to be,” Burnham said.
Much of Burnham’s speech addressed the need for social reforms with a focus on caregivers and healthcare, including building a “National Care Service … free at the point of use”.
He said it will be “a person-centred, high-quality” service where “everyone contributes and everyone is covered” and care “is about people not profit”, does not erode savings and gives “proper recognition” to care workers.
There was also talk of adjusting the so-called “pension triple lock” that sets state pension rises. He said changes will be made by April 2030, after the next general election.
Burnham said low-income pensioners would not ⁠pay income tax in the current Parliament. The planned changes meant pensioners would receive annual rises to their state pension without ‌additional care charges, “so that pensioners will always share in ⁠the rising prosperity of the nation”.
He also spoke on the need to make housing more affordable, confirming his party’s intention to make it easy for young people to own a home by reducing the deposit needed to buy property.
There was also mention of returning control of utilities, such as water and electricity, back to the public, by scrapping “[former Prime Minister] Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”.
On electricity, Burnham announced a new publicly-owned “Great British Grid” that will “challenge the private sector operators” to “increase competition, drive down costs and speed up delivery”, and make it easier to connect to the electricity grid.
Burnham’s speech also focused on foreign policy issues, saying he will “stand up to” Russian and Iranian “threats”.
“I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine and stand up to threats wherever they come from, whether Russia, Iran, or anywhere,” he said.
On Israel, the occupied West Bank and Gaza, Burnham praised his foreign secretary’s approach, since assuming office in July.
“We will be principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband has done,” he said.
Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic, who was listening to the British prime minister at the conference, said Burnham’s speech was laced with “a lot of fiery rhetoric”.
“Britain finds itself in a very dire position when it comes to finances,” said Veselinovic, adding that there is immense pressure on Burnham’s new government as it prepares to introduce its first budget at the end of October.
The UK annual consumer price inflation (CPI) reached 3.1 percent in the 12 months to August, ticking up from 2.9 percent in July, according to the Office of National Statistics.
Veselinovic said Burnham is aware he may have to “pay a political price for all the reforms he’s promising”, but that he also understands, “somebody has to rip out the plaster on that because the costs are too high”.
Danny Sriskandarajah, the chief executive officer of New Economics Foundation, said Burnham delivered “a remarkable speech”.
“Andy Burnham has this knack to be able to come across as authentic, as genuine,” Sriskandarajah told Al Jazeera.
Burnham, Sriskandarajah said, “was tearful at moments”.
“He was honest about what challenges Britain faces. But he also generates a sense of hope which I think is much needed,” he said.
Sriskandarajah said the challenge for Burnham will be to fund the promises he made in the speech.
“All of these things that he wants to do will cost money, which means they’ll have to raise those resources somewhere,” he said.

The Boston Red Sox found a way to make it to the postseason after a disastrous start to the season. They were just 9-17 on Friday, April 24, and that was their fourth straight loss, all to AL East opponents. They ended up firing their manager, but things really didn't improve all that much. They were 29-43 around the middle of June. Then, almost like a light switch, they found a way to start winning.
From June 25 until the end of the season, the team went 55-29. Over the course of a full 162-game season, that would give them almost 110 wins. It was one of the best runs in their history.

He was better on the road than he was at home with a 2.50 road ERA and a .202 opposing batting average. He was also spectacular against the Yankees this season, going 13.0 innings in two starts and allowing just four hits and one earned run while striking out 18 hitters.

articles.title_orig: South Korea says North Korean mines behind DMZ blast violated armistice
articles.title_zh: South Korea says North Korean mines behind DMZ blast violated armistice
articles.content_orig:
The blasts that wounded three South Korean soldiers last week were apparently caused by North Korean mines, Seoul said on Tuesday, adding it was an armistice violation that would prompt "corresponding measures."
One troop lost a foot due to the explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world's most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul's comments came a day after his ministry said North Korean mines were "highly suspected" of causing the two explosions last week.
"This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures," he told a parliamentary hearing, when asked whether the military had tentatively concluded that the mine was North Korean.
Kang said South Korean forces were in the DMZ to clear the area in advance of an operation with the UN Command to assess terrain changes caused by North Korean forces south of the Military Demarcation Line, which marks the nations' effective border.
The mine detectors used by the officials were the "latest models," the minister said, but detection efforts were hampered by dense vegetation in the area, noting that "clearing all the vegetation as they advanced was difficult."
"Our current assessment is that the mines may not have been detected because the detectors were being operated too far above the ground," he said.
At the hearing, Yang Jin-hyeok of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told lawmakers that a site investigation earlier on Tuesday discovered an unexploded North Korean plastic anti-personnel mine.
Kang told lawmakers the military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages", without giving details.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in a truce, not a peace treaty.
Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, said on Monday that two landmines exploded during the 21 September incident and that a third, unexploded mine was found while soldiers were withdrawing after the blast.
"Taking into account the crater and the pattern of the flames from the explosion, the extent of the injuries sustained by the service members...we assess that North Korean landmines are highly suspected to have caused the blast," Kwon said at the time.
Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country's "principal enemy," Pyongyang's military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.
In a 2015 landmine incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.
Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the Military Demarcation Line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.
The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts along the border.

President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order on Monday that raises the strength of the Russian military by 15,500 troops, bringing the total number of active-duty servicemen to 1.55 million.
Putin has raised the number of military personnel several times since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Monday’s order does not explain the reason for the latest increase. The Russian military’s total strength now stands at 2,441,630 personnel.
This year, the military has created 52,500 new positions, according to the exiled news outlet Meduza, the vast majority of which are active-duty military slots rather than civilian support staff.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preparing for a new mass mobilization of troops after holding parliamentary elections last week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky c laimed Russia has “in effect” begun the process of surging troop recruitment “through various means,” though he did not provide details.
Putin, who last ordered a “partial” mobilization of reservists in September 2022, has dismissed the mobilization claims as “disinformation.”
Some military experts have argued that the Kremlin is unlikely to issue a new draft order like in 2022 due to the fact that “partial” mobilization remains in effect.
Others have cautioned that another mass call-up of service-age men would encounter logistical hurdles and fail to address challenges on the front line.
